# Nonlinear and fluid suites: declared contracts and their walls {#sec-nonlinear-suites}

The exact-kernel MeshTransformer (MT1, @sec-mt1) states its contracts
for linear operators: drive linearity, zero preservation, parity typing,
similarity equivariance. The five suites in this chapter measure what
happens when the operator is nonlinear, when labels come from a solver
instead of a closed form, and when a Reynolds number grades the
nonlinearity continuously. The result is uniform across the suites: **a
declared contract that matches the problem costs nothing or helps; a
contract that mismatches the problem produces an exact, often provable
wall; and every wall measured here was crossed by declaring a different
contract, never by adding capacity.** The chapter also records where the
declarations stop paying: a nonlinear read-in whose implicit polynomial
degree detonates off-range, a zero-preservation contract that is exactly
wrong on a problem whose homogeneous solution is nonzero, and a viscous
suite where the declared degree is only an approximation.

## Why nonlinear suites, and what each one tests

The linear suites (@sec-linear-suites) cannot falsify linearity as an
assumption, because their solution operators are linear. Each suite here
removes one thing the linear contracts rely on. Throughout, the *drive*
is everything the model receives besides geometry: the boundary trace
and any global scalars or vectors (a freestream direction, a
circulation, a PDE coefficient). The *drive degree* of a target is the
polynomial degree of the solution map in the drive at fixed geometry.
MT1's decoder reads the drive through one of three declared *field
modes*: the linear mode (output exactly linear in the drive), a
zero-preserving nonlinear mode (multiplicative updates that read drive
invariants, zero output at zero drive, no degree bound), and a
declared-degree mode (the linear path plus exactly one bilinear
composition at the query read-in, so the output is a polynomial of
degree at most two in the drive for any weights). Parity typing adds an
optional sector of two-dimensional pseudoscalar (mirror-odd) channels
(@sec-typed-channels); "parity channels" below always means that sector.

| suite | PDE and target | label source | what the model sees | evaluation | what it tests |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Liouville | $\Delta u + 2e^{u} = 0$ on star-deformed disks; scalar $u$ | closed form (spherical-metric potentials) | Dirichlet trace on 64 panels; 128 queries | streamed training, 1,500 steps, 3 seeds; 16 cases per split | nonlinearity with exact labels; the superposition wall; zero preservation as a misspecified contract |
| potential flow | $\Delta\psi = 0$ outside a body; streamfunction or velocity | closed form (exterior conformal maps) | body outline on 160 panels, freestream vector, circulation scalar; 256 queries | 3,000 steps, 3 or 5 seeds; 16 cases per split | vector drive; handed (pseudoscalar) targets; trace-driven versus raw-drive inputs |
| Euler–Bernoulli | same flows; velocity (degree 1) and Bernoulli pressure (degree 2) | closed form | as potential flow | 3,000 steps, 3 or 5 seeds | two fields of known, different drive degree in one sample |
| rotational Euler | $\Delta\psi = -\tilde c^{2}\psi$ on disks; velocity and pressure | closed form (Bessel series; momentum balance certified to $10^{-15}$) | boundary velocity on 64 panels, coupling $\tilde c$; 128 queries | 3,000 steps, 3 seeds; 16 cases per split | vortical flow with exact labels; an operator parameter approaching a resonance |
| Navier–Stokes cavity | steady incompressible Navier–Stokes; velocity and pressure | Taylor–Hood P2–P1 finite elements, per-case certification | tangential wall drive on 64 panels, $1/\mathrm{Re}$; 160 queries | fixed catalog of 1,400 cases (840 train), 15 epochs, 3 seeds | solver labels with a measured noise floor; nonlinearity graded by Reynolds number |

: The five suites, in the order the chapter treats them. Geometry
families and split definitions are those of @sec-datasets. "Streamed
training" draws a fresh case every step from the generator; the
Navier–Stokes suite is the only one with a fixed catalog. {#tbl-nonlinear-suites}

The metric everywhere is the relative $L^2$ error of a field over the
query points of one case, $\|\hat u - u\| / \|u\|$, averaged
arithmetically over the evaluation cases of a split. Where a suite has
two fields, "combined" concatenates velocity and pressure before taking
the norm. The parameter-free reference in every table that records it
is the *boundary-mean predictor*: the mean of the boundary trace,
returned at every query. Every MT1 arm in this chapter uses the one-head
configuration and the two-member exact kernel dictionary (double-layer
and single-layer members, @sec-kernel-decoder); arms differ only in the
declared field mode and in whether parity channels are on.

The figure below shows, on the Liouville suite, why a nonlinear operator
defeats the linear contract: two exact solutions on the same domain sum
to a field that is not a solution.

```{python}
#| label: fig-nonlinear-superposition
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Why the linear contract fails on a nonlinear operator, rendered live
#|   from the Liouville generator. Left and center: two exact solutions on
#|   the same star-deformed domain (interior field with the boundary trace
#|   drawn on top; shared color scale); each satisfies the PDE to machine
#|   precision. Right: the PDE residual of their sum, which the equation
#|   gives in closed form as $2(e^{u_1+u_2} - e^{u_1} - e^{u_2})$. It is
#|   nonzero, so the sum of two solutions is not a solution, and a model
#|   whose output is linear in the boundary data cannot be exact. For a
#|   linear suite this panel would be identically zero. Not shown: any
#|   model output. Generator: `problems/liouville.py`.
#| code-fold: true
import json
import math
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib as mpl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import torch
from matplotlib.collections import LineCollection
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap, Normalize
from matplotlib.tri import Triangulation

# book palette (mirrors figures.py without importing it: that module
# switches matplotlib to Agg, which suppresses inline output here)
BLUE, RED = "#2a78d6", "#e34948"
INK, INK2, MUTED, GRID, BASELINE = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9", "#c3c2b7"
mpl.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 10, "axes.edgecolor": BASELINE,
                     "axes.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID,
                     "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "xtick.labelcolor": INK2,
                     "ytick.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.spines.top": False,
                     "axes.spines.right": False, "legend.frameon": False})
# architecture hues: exact-kernel MeshTransformer purple, Transolver grey.
# MT1 arms that differ only by declared contract share the hue and are
# separated by lightness and marker.
PURPLE, PURPLE_LIGHT, PURPLE_DARK = "#7b4fb3", "#b89ad9", "#4b2c7f"
TRANSOLVER = "#52514e"
DIVERGING = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list(
    "book_diverging", ["#2a78d6", "#f0efec", "#e34948"])
SEQ_PURPLE = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list(
    "book_seq_purple", ["#f0efec", PURPLE])

RESULTS = Path("..") / "results"


def direct_labels(ax, items, x_text, min_gap, log_y=True, fontsize=7.5):
    """Label line ends directly instead of with a legend.

    items: (x_end, y_end, text, color) for each line. Every label sits in
    one column at data x = x_text; labels are pushed apart vertically (in
    log10 units if log_y) so they do not overlap, and a thin leader joins
    each label to its line end.
    """
    items = sorted(items, key=lambda t: t[1])
    ys = [math.log10(y) if log_y else y for _, y, _, _ in items]
    for i in range(1, len(ys)):
        if ys[i] - ys[i - 1] < min_gap:
            ys[i] = ys[i - 1] + min_gap
    # keep the stack inside the axes: cap at the top, then push down
    lo, hi = ax.get_ylim()
    top = (math.log10(hi) if log_y else hi) - 0.6 * min_gap
    if ys[-1] > top:
        ys[-1] = top
        for i in range(len(ys) - 2, -1, -1):
            ys[i] = min(ys[i], ys[i + 1] - min_gap)
    for (x, y0, text, color), y in zip(items, ys):
        ax.annotate(text, (x, y0), xytext=(x_text, 10 ** y if log_y else y),
                    textcoords="data", fontsize=fontsize, color=color, va="center",
                    ha="left", annotation_clip=False,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=color, lw=0.6, alpha=0.6,
                                    shrinkA=0, shrinkB=2))


import warnings

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # the generators import physicsnemo.experimental
for _entry in (Path("..").resolve(), Path("..").resolve() / "problems"):
    if str(_entry) not in sys.path:
        sys.path.insert(0, str(_entry))
from conformal_laplace import conformal_map
from liouville import (
    build_liouville_sample,
    liouville_solution,
    sample_liouville_field,
)


def disk_triangulation(n_rings=28, n_theta=96):
    radii = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, n_rings + 1)[1:]
    theta = np.linspace(0.0, 2.0 * np.pi, n_theta, endpoint=False)
    points = [np.zeros((1, 2))]
    for r in radii:
        points.append(np.stack([r * np.cos(theta), r * np.sin(theta)], axis=1))
    points = np.concatenate(points)
    triangles = [[0, 1 + j, 1 + (j + 1) % n_theta] for j in range(n_theta)]
    for i in range(n_rings - 1):
        a, b = 1 + i * n_theta, 1 + (i + 1) * n_theta
        for j in range(n_theta):
            k = (j + 1) % n_theta
            triangles += [[a + j, b + j, b + k], [a + j, b + k, a + k]]
    return points, np.array(triangles)


sample = build_liouville_sample(5)
geometry, field_1 = sample.geometry, sample.field
radius_bound = float(1.0 + geometry.coefficients.abs().sum().item())
pre_points, triangles = disk_triangulation()
z_grid = torch.complex(torch.tensor(pre_points[:, 0]), torch.tensor(pre_points[:, 1]))
physical = conformal_map(geometry, z_grid)
angles = torch.linspace(0.0, 2.0 * math.pi, 257, dtype=torch.float64)
ring = conformal_map(geometry, torch.polar(torch.ones_like(angles), angles))
ring_xy = torch.stack((ring.real, ring.imag), dim=-1).numpy()
ring_mid = 0.5 * (ring[:-1] + ring[1:])

u1 = liouville_solution(field_1, physical).numpy()
field_2 = None
for candidate_seed in range(1000, 1200):
    candidate = sample_liouville_field(candidate_seed, domain_radius_bound=radius_bound)
    u2 = liouville_solution(candidate, physical).numpy()
    if np.abs(u2).max() <= 4.0 and u2.max() - u2.min() >= 2.0:
        field_2 = candidate
        break
if field_2 is None:
    raise RuntimeError("no admissible second Liouville field found")
residual = 2.0 * (np.exp(u1 + u2) - np.exp(u1) - np.exp(u2))

u_amp = max(np.abs(u1).max(), np.abs(u2).max())
u_norm = Normalize(-u_amp, u_amp)
r_amp = np.abs(residual).max()
r_norm = Normalize(-r_amp, r_amp)

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9.2, 3.6))
grid = fig.add_gridspec(1, 3, left=0.02, right=0.84, top=0.88, bottom=0.10, wspace=0.08)
panels = [
    (u1, u_norm, r"$u_1$ (exact solution)", r"residual $\equiv 0$"),
    (u2, u_norm, r"$u_2$ (exact, same domain)", r"residual $\equiv 0$"),
    (residual, r_norm, r"$\Delta(u_1{+}u_2) + 2e^{u_1+u_2}$", r"residual $\neq 0$: not a solution"),
]
for col, (values, norm, title, note) in enumerate(panels):
    ax = fig.add_subplot(grid[0, col])
    tri = Triangulation(physical.real.numpy(), physical.imag.numpy(), triangles)
    cs = ax.tricontourf(tri, values, levels=np.linspace(norm.vmin, norm.vmax, 27),
                        cmap=DIVERGING, alpha=0.82)
    cs.set_edgecolor("face")
    if col < 2:
        trace = liouville_solution(field_1 if col == 0 else field_2, ring_mid)
        segments = np.stack([ring_xy[:-1], ring_xy[1:]], axis=1)
        ax.add_collection(LineCollection(
            segments, colors=DIVERGING(norm(trace.numpy())), linewidths=3.2,
            zorder=4, capstyle="round"))
    else:
        ax.plot(ring_xy[:, 0], ring_xy[:, 1], color=INK, lw=2.4, zorder=4)
    ax.text(0.5, -0.04, note, transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top",
            fontsize=8.5, color=INK2 if col < 2 else INK)
    lo, hi = ring_xy.min(axis=0), ring_xy.max(axis=0)
    mid, half = (lo + hi) / 2, (hi - lo).max() / 2 * 1.10
    ax.set_xlim(mid[0] - half, mid[0] + half)
    ax.set_ylim(mid[1] - half, mid[1] + half)
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
    for spine in ax.spines.values():
        spine.set_visible(False)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10, color=INK)
cax_u = fig.add_axes([0.865, 0.18, 0.016, 0.55])
cbar = fig.colorbar(plt.cm.ScalarMappable(cmap=DIVERGING, norm=u_norm), cax=cax_u)
cbar.set_label(r"$u$  [-]", fontsize=8); cbar.ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
cax_r = fig.add_axes([0.945, 0.18, 0.016, 0.55])
cbar = fig.colorbar(plt.cm.ScalarMappable(cmap=DIVERGING, norm=r_norm), cax=cax_r)
cbar.set_label("residual  [-]", fontsize=8); cbar.ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
plt.show()
```

## The nonlinear-fragility ladder: implicit degree diagnosed, then declared {#sec-nonlinear-fragility}

**The zero-preserving nonlinear read-in carries an implicit drive degree
near 21, which is invisible on the training range and detonates off it;
declaring the degree removes the mechanism rather than damping it.**
This is the single most consequential finding of the nonlinear suites,
because it decides which field mode is safe to deploy wherever the drive
can leave its training range, including the industrial datasets
(@sec-industrial-mt1).

The diagnosis rests on one probe: scale the joint drive by a factor
$\alpha$ at fixed geometry and fit the log-log slope of the output's RMS
against $\alpha$. For a target of drive degree $d$ the exact slope is
$d$. On Euler–Bernoulli arms trained in the nonlinear mode, the fitted
slope over the training band $\alpha \in [0.5, 1.5]$ is 1.56 for the
velocity (target 1) and 3.82 for the pressure (target 2); over the
extrapolation band $\alpha \in [2, 4]$ it is **21.3 and 20.8**. Training
suppresses the spurious high-degree terms where the data lives and
nowhere else; a snapshot at step 200 already reads 18.1 and 17.4, so the
degree is built in from initialization. Two rival explanations were
excluded on the rotational-Euler suite, whose nonlinear arms fail by
$10^{6}$–$10^{13}$ near the operator's first eigenvalue
(@sec-euler-rotational). Sweeping the coupling through that band at a
pinned drive moves nothing in the conditioned stack (worst ratio of
near-eigenvalue to training-band activations 1.61), so operator
conditioning is not the failure. Renormalizing the near-eigenvalue cases
by their known physical amplification (dividing velocity by $A$ and
pressure by $A^2$, which leaves them exact solutions) brings the same
checkpoint from $5.6\times10^{6}$ to 0.240. The parameter-axis failure
is the amplitude axis in disguise: the operator amplifies the drive by up
to 77 times, and $1.6^{21}$ is already $2\times10^{4}$.

The fix declares the degree the way linearity is declared. The
declared-degree mode keeps the linear path end to end (drive lift, linear
field blocks, linear kernel decode) and adds exactly one bilinear,
operator-conditioned composition at the query read-in,
$F = u + B(L_2 u, L_3 u)$. Every learned ingredient is linear in the
drive, bilinear in the drive, or drive-independent, so the output is a
polynomial of degree at most two for any weights. The composition sits at
the read-in rather than in a stackable block because residual bilinear
updates would compose to degree $2^k$, which is the escalation the mode
exists to forbid. The acceptance test is the diagnosis probe run on the
trained checkpoints in float64: fitted slopes of 1.00 (velocity) and
2.00 (pressure) on- and off-range on every seed of both suites, and the
exact polynomial $c_1\alpha + c_2\alpha^2$ reproduces the model to a
worst relative residual of $2.1\times10^{-15}$. The same probe on the
nonlinear mode fails by eleven orders of magnitude, so the contract is a
discriminating unit test, not a metric.

```{python}
#| label: fig-declared-degree
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The implicit degree and its removal. Left: velocity RMS response to
#|   joint drive scaling at fixed geometry on trained Euler–Bernoulli
#|   arms, log-log (case 0 of each artifact). The nonlinear read-in tracks
#|   the exact degree-1 response on the training range and leaves it at
#|   slope near 21 beyond alpha of about 1.5; the declared-degree arm's
#|   response is a degree-2 polynomial (fit residual 2e-15) and is
#|   indistinguishable from the exact slope at every alpha. Right:
#|   rotational-Euler combined relative L2 error versus the vorticity
#|   coupling; the nonlinear arm (one seed) detonates approaching the
#|   first eigenvalue while the declared-degree arm (3-seed mean, band =
#|   seed range) stays below 1.0 on cases the linear arm handles at about
#|   0.2. How to read this: both panels probe trained checkpoints; neither
#|   shows in-distribution accuracy, which @tbl-euler-bernoulli and
#|   @tbl-euler-rotational carry. Data: results/nonlinear_fragility_2026-07-04.json,
#|   results/declared_degree_2026-07-05.json.
#| code-fold: true
diagnosis = json.load(open(RESULTS / "nonlinear_fragility_2026-07-04.json"))
fix = json.load(open(RESULTS / "declared_degree_2026-07-05.json"))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 3.9))
nl_rows = diagnosis["eb_amplitude_cases"][0]["rows"]
q2_rows = fix["results"]["euler_bernoulli"]["per_seed"][0]["amplitude_probe_cases"][0]["rows"]
alphas = [r["alpha"] for r in nl_rows]
ax = axes[0]
exact_rms = [r["velocity_exact_rms"] for r in nl_rows]
nl_rms = [r["velocity_rms"] for r in nl_rows]
q2_alphas, q2_rms = [r["alpha"] for r in q2_rows], [r["velocity_rms"] for r in q2_rows]
ax.loglog(alphas, exact_rms, "--", color=INK, lw=2.0, zorder=4)
ax.loglog(alphas, nl_rms, "o-", ms=3.5, color=PURPLE, lw=1.2)
ax.loglog(q2_alphas, q2_rms, "s-", ms=3.5, color=PURPLE_DARK, lw=1.2)
ax.axvspan(2.0, 4.0, color=GRID, alpha=0.5, zorder=0)
ax.text(2.8, 2e-2, "extrapolated\nband", fontsize=7.5, ha="center", color=INK2)
direct_labels(ax, [
    (alphas[-1], nl_rms[-1], "MT1, nonlinear read-in\n(slope 21.3 off-range)", PURPLE_DARK),
    (q2_alphas[-1], q2_rms[-1], "MT1, declared degree 2", PURPLE_DARK),
    (alphas[-1], exact_rms[-1], "exact (degree 1)", INK),
], x_text=alphas[-1] * 1.12, min_gap=0.55)
ax.set_xlim(right=alphas[-1] * 3.4)
ax.set_xlabel(r"drive scale $\alpha$ [-]")
ax.set_ylabel("velocity RMS response [-]")
ax.set_title("Euler–Bernoulli: the degree probe", fontsize=9)

nl_sweep = diagnosis["er_amplification_sweep"]
q2_sweeps = [entry["amplification_sweep"] for entry in fix["results"]["euler_rotational"]["per_seed"]]
couplings = [e["coupling"] for e in nl_sweep]
q2_matrix = np.array([[e["mean_combined"] for e in sweep] for sweep in q2_sweeps])
ax = axes[1]
nl_combined = [e["mean_combined"] for e in nl_sweep]
q2_mean_curve = q2_matrix.mean(axis=0)
ax.semilogy(couplings, nl_combined, "o-", ms=3.5, color=PURPLE, lw=1.2)
ax.semilogy(couplings, q2_mean_curve, "s-", ms=3.5, color=PURPLE_DARK, lw=1.2)
ax.fill_between(couplings, q2_matrix.min(axis=0), q2_matrix.max(axis=0), color=PURPLE_DARK,
                alpha=0.2, lw=0)
ax.axhline(1.0, color=INK, lw=1.0, ls="--")
ax.text(1.02, 1.3, "acceptance bar (1.0)", fontsize=7.5, color=INK, va="bottom")
ax.axvline(2.4048, color=INK2, lw=1.0, ls=":")
ax.text(2.39, 3e-2, r"$j_{0,1}$", fontsize=8, ha="right", color=INK2)
direct_labels(ax, [
    (couplings[-1], nl_combined[-1], "MT1, nonlinear read-in\n(one seed)", PURPLE_DARK),
], x_text=2.5, min_gap=1.2)
ax.annotate("MT1, declared degree 2\n(3-seed mean, band = range)", (couplings[-1], q2_mean_curve[-1]),
            xytext=(2.5, 0.3), textcoords="data", fontsize=7.5, color=PURPLE_DARK, va="top",
            ha="left", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=PURPLE_DARK, lw=0.6, alpha=0.6,
                                       shrinkA=0, shrinkB=2))
ax.set_xlim(right=3.45)
ax.set_xlabel(r"vorticity coupling $\tilde c$ [-]")
ax.set_ylabel("combined relative $L^2$ [-] (log)")
ax.set_title("rotational Euler: error vs operator parameter", fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

What declaring the degree buys, and what it costs, at matched parity
typing:

- The detonation is gone, not damped. The rotational near-eigenvalue
  tier falls from $10^{6}$–$10^{13}$ to 0.670 ± 0.111 combined; the
  unseen-mode split from 160 ± 178 to 0.144 ± 0.013. Parity channels
  alone had reduced the detonation by orders of magnitude without
  removing it; the declared degree removes the exploding monomials by
  construction.
- In-distribution accuracy is not the price. The declared-degree arms
  are more accurate in-distribution than the nonlinear arms on both
  exact-label suites (rotational Euler velocity/pressure 0.037/0.106 vs
  0.061/0.181; Euler–Bernoulli with parity channels 0.029/0.035 vs
  0.031/0.063) and far more seed-stable off-range (Euler–Bernoulli
  circulation-OOD seed spread 0.003 vs 0.40 without parity channels).
- Degree and parity are orthogonal declarations, and the amplitude axis
  needs both. Without parity channels the declared-degree arm's
  circulation-OOD is pinned at 0.682, the parity floor of
  @sec-ds-potential-flow; with them it reaches 0.086 ± 0.059 against the
  nonlinear-with-parity arm's 0.35.
- What remains is amplitude, not degree. On the near-eigenvalue tier the
  declared-degree velocity reaches 0.216, the level of the renormalized
  probe, while the pressure, amplified by $A^2$ of 150–6,000, sits at
  0.686. The structural probe on the same checkpoints shows no response
  above degree two.
- The cost appears where the true degree is unbounded. On Navier–Stokes
  every polynomial order is present in the solution map, and the
  declared-degree arm trails the nonlinear arm in-distribution (0.278 vs
  0.231 combined, @tbl-ns-arms): there the declaration is an
  approximation hypothesis, and a degree-2 truncation is measurably
  short.

## The fluid suites with exact labels: potential flow and Euler–Bernoulli {#sec-fluid-suites}

These two suites share one exterior-flow family and add, in turn, a
vector drive with a handed target and a second target of a different
drive degree. Both are linear or polynomial in the drive with exact
labels, so every wall in them is a theorem the tables confirm.

### Potential flow {#sec-ds-potential-flow}

**Given the same inputs as a trace-informed control, MT1 (about 105k
parameters) solves the exterior problem with circulation to relative
error 0.013 where the 19,008-parameter pair-kernel control, which
receives the same exact boundary trace as per-cell input, reaches 0.178;
given only the raw drive, MT1 is at no-response on a streamfunction
target, by a parity argument, and the fix is a typed channel, not
capacity.** Smooth
two-dimensional bodies (conformal images of the unit circle, restricted to
orientation-preserving placements) sit in a uniform stream $U_\infty$
with prescribed circulation $\Gamma$. The exact flow is classical
potential theory: $\Delta\psi = 0$ outside the body, $\psi = 0$ on it,
$\nabla\psi \to U_\infty^{\perp}$ at infinity. Splits: in-distribution,
unseen geometry modes, wilder shapes (deformation bound 0.45–0.70
against the training 0.05–0.35), circulation beyond the training band,
and far-field queries beyond the training annulus.

The primary target, the disturbance streamfunction $\psi_d$, is a
two-dimensional *pseudoscalar*: reflect the whole problem in a mirror and
the exact solution is the mirrored field with its sign flipped, because
the uniform-flow part is the wedge $U_x y - U_y x$. Every quantity MT1's
default type system builds from dot products of polar vectors is a true
scalar, equal to its mirror image. An untyped model therefore predicts
the same field for a problem and its mirror image, and the best it can do
is the even part of the target.

```{python}
#| label: fig-potential-parity
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The parity wall, drawn from the exact generator. Left: a circulatory
#|   flow (filled streamfunction). Right: the mirrored problem, with
#|   reflected geometry, reflected freestream and negated circulation,
#|   whose exact solution is the reflected field with opposite sign. Every
#|   dot-product invariant of geometry and drive is identical for the two
#|   problems, so an untyped model must predict the same field for both.
#|   Not shown: any model output. Generator: `problems/potential_flow.py`.
#| code-fold: true
from potential_flow import (
    body_to_physical,
    build_potential_flow_sample,
    complex_to_points,
    total_streamfunction,
)

sample = build_potential_flow_sample(6, dtype=torch.float64)
radii = torch.linspace(1.0005, 2.6, 80, dtype=torch.float64)[None, :]
angles = torch.linspace(0.0, 2 * np.pi, 240, dtype=torch.float64)[:, None]
z = (radii * torch.exp(1j * angles)).to(torch.complex128)
psi = total_streamfunction(sample.body, sample.canonical_freestream, 1.4, z).numpy()
phys = complex_to_points(body_to_physical(sample.body, z)).numpy()
X, Y = phys[..., 0], phys[..., 1]
span = np.abs(psi).max()
loop = sample.boundary_loop.numpy()

fig, (axa, axb) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.2, 4.4))
for ax, (Xp, Yp, P, label) in zip(
        (axa, axb),
        ((X, Y, psi, "flow with circulation $+\\Gamma$"),
         (X, -Y, -psi, "mirrored problem: exact answer is $-\\Gamma$"))):
    ax.contourf(Xp, Yp, P, levels=np.linspace(-span, span, 27), cmap=DIVERGING)
    ax.contour(Xp, Yp, P, levels=np.linspace(-span, span, 27), colors="#00000022", linewidths=0.5)
    yy = loop[:, 1] if Yp is Y else -loop[:, 1]
    ax.fill(loop[:, 0], yy, facecolor="#eae8e1", edgecolor=INK, linewidth=1.6, zorder=3)
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
    for spine in ax.spines.values():
        spine.set_visible(False)
    ax.set_title(label, fontsize=10, color=INK)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The control semantics matter more here than anywhere else in the book.
The *pair-kernel control* is a learned two-point kernel of 19,008
parameters that receives the exact disturbance trace as per-cell boundary
data; it is *trace-informed*. The raw-drive MT1 arms (about 105k–113k
parameters, depending on the dictionary) receive only the body outline,
$U_\infty$ and $\Gamma$, and must reconstruct the trace themselves. A
trace-driven arm
therefore holds strictly more information than a raw-drive arm, and the
two must never be compared as equals: the trace-informed row is a
reference for what the *data* supports, not a competitor. The table
reports 3-seed means of the relative $L^2$ error of $\psi_d$ after 3,000
streamed steps.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-potential-flow
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
bie = json.load(open(RESULTS / "learned_bie_2026-07-02.json"))
it21 = bie["iteration_21_fluid_families_pseudoscalar_wall"]["runs_partial"]
it22 = bie["iteration_22_representable_reformulations"]["runs"]
pf_splits = [("in_distribution", "in-distribution"), ("unseen_geometry_modes", "unseen geometry"),
             ("wilder_shapes", "wilder shapes"), ("circulation_ood", "circulation OOD"),
             ("farfield_queries", "far-field")]


def split_means(runs):
    return {k: sum(r[k] for r in runs) / len(runs) for k, _ in pf_splits}


def row(label, runs, bold=False):
    m = split_means(runs)
    cells = " | ".join(f"{m[k]:.3f}" for k, _ in pf_splits)
    return f"| {label} | {cells} |"


lines = ["| arm (3-seed means) | " + " | ".join(n for _, n in pf_splits) + " |",
         "|---|" + "--:|" * len(pf_splits)]
lines.append(row("MT1, raw drive $\\{U_\\infty, \\Gamma\\}$, streamfunction target (no response)",
                 it21["potential_flow_mesh_transformer_kernel"]))
lines.append(row("pair-kernel control, trace-informed", it21["potential_flow_pair_kernel"]))
lines.append(": Exterior potential flow, streamfunction target: relative $L^2$ "
             "error, 3,000 steps, seeds 17/18/19. The raw-drive arm sits at "
             "no-response on every seed (in-distribution 0.98–1.00) although a "
             "gradient diagnostic shows the drive path is alive; the output cannot "
             "be handed. The control's 0.178 is what the trace supports, not a "
             "matched comparison. Data: results/learned_bie_2026-07-02.json, key "
             "`iteration_21_fluid_families_pseudoscalar_wall`. {#tbl-potential-flow}")
print("\n".join(lines))
```

Two reformulations make the target representable. *Trace-driven* MT1
arms receive the same certified trace as the control, so the handedness
arrives in the data; they predict $\psi_d$. *Velocity* arms keep the raw
drive and change the target to the flow velocity, a polar vector, which
the type system represents as-is.

Three facts follow. Given identical data, the trace-driven MT1 arm
(about 105k parameters) reaches 0.013 in-distribution and 0.020 on
circulation-OOD against 0.178 for the 19,008-parameter pair-kernel
control, both fed the exact boundary trace; the 5.5x parameter gap
between them is a caveat on the size of the margin, not on its sign, and
the encode-and-solve path handles the exterior problem with circulation;
the wall was target type alone. The velocity arms fit
(0.14 in-distribution) but their circulation-OOD is pinned at
0.646–0.649 across every arm and seed, a spread too tight for optimization
noise: the vortex velocity is $\Gamma\,x^{\perp}/(2\pi|x|^2)$, and with
$\Gamma$ typed as a true scalar that product is an axial vector the
system cannot represent, so the error is exactly the norm of the vortex
component. Adding the pseudoscalar channel sector (wedge products and
rotations as typed operations, circulation declared odd) removes that
exclusion:

```{python}

```

The two exact members remain the best dictionary under the extension.
The far-field column is the weakest split for every arm in all three
tables: it measures radial extrapolation beyond the training annulus,
a question about exterior decay rather than about nonlinearity, and is
not pursued in this chapter. Parity channels are two-dimensional and
opt-in; the three-dimensional analogue (axial vectors) is out of scope.

### Euler–Bernoulli: two fields, two drive degrees {#sec-ds-euler-bernoulli}

**A linear-mode arm's pressure error is exactly 1.000 on every split and
seed, by parity, while the same arm's velocity is fine; declaring
nonlinearity breaks the wall and composing it with parity channels wins
every column.** The suite reuses the exterior-flow family with two
targets at shared queries: the velocity $u = U_\infty + u_d$, a polar
vector of drive degree 1, and the Bernoulli pressure
$p^{*} = \tfrac12(|U_\infty|^2 - |u|^2)$, exactly degree 2. The labels
are exact and mutually consistent. Because the drive distribution is
symmetric under negation, every degree-2 target is orthogonal to the
span of any drive-linear model, whose best pressure prediction is
therefore zero.


The two declared mechanisms fix different deficits and compose: the
nonlinear mode breaks the degree wall (pressure 1.000 to 0.210) and the
parity channels carry the handedness, and the composed arm is 5x and 3x

## Rotational Euler and Liouville

### Rotational Euler: exact vorticity and an operator parameter {#sec-ds-euler-rotational}

**Where the velocity map is exactly drive-linear, the linear mode is the
best velocity model (0.026, 2.3x better than nonlinear mode) and degrades
gracefully on every axis; the nonlinear mode buys the pressure at a
velocity cost and detonates near the operator's eigenvalue.** Disks with
randomized radius, center and panel rotation carry boundary velocity for
a steady two-dimensional Euler flow with vorticity proportional to the
streamfunction, $\omega = \tilde c^{2}\psi$. The streamfunction then
solves the Helmholtz equation $\Delta\psi + \tilde c^{2}\psi = 0$, whose
Bessel-series solutions on a disk are exact; the velocity is
$\nabla^{\perp}\psi$ (degree 1 in the drive) and the pressure follows
from the rotational Bernoulli relation, $p = -\tilde c^{2}\psi^{2}/2 -
|u|^{2}/2$, exactly degree 2. Float64 autograd puts the steady-Euler
momentum residual of every label at $10^{-16}$ to $10^{-15}$. The model
sees the boundary velocity as a rank-1 drive on 64 panels and the
dimensionless coupling $\tilde c$ as a global operator scalar, nothing
else. Splits: in-distribution ($\tilde c \in [0.5, 1.8]$, drive modes
0–3), unseen coupling ($[1.9, 2.2]$), unseen modes (4–6), and a
near-eigenvalue tier ($[2.25, 2.38]$) retained because its labels stay
exact.

The coupling has a hard ceiling. At the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of
the disk, $j_{0,1} \approx 2.405$, the homogeneous problem acquires a
nonzero solution and the interior is no longer determined by boundary
data; approaching it, the interior response to unit boundary data grows
like $1/J_0(\tilde c)$, up to about 77x at the band edge.

```{python}
#| label: fig-er-amplification
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The resonance dial: interior response amplitude (maximum of the
#|   exact target over a fixed-seed sample with unit-RMS boundary data) as
#|   the coupling approaches the first Dirichlet eigenvalue (dotted line),
#|   with the three coupling splits shaded. The near-eigenvalue band's
#|   amplification is what the fragility ladder measured accuracy against.
#|   Not shown: any model output. Generator: `problems/euler_rotational.py`.
#| code-fold: true
from euler_rotational import build_euler_rotational_sample

couplings = np.linspace(0.5, 2.39, 28)
amplitudes = []
for c in couplings:
    s = build_euler_rotational_sample(11, coupling_range=(float(c), float(c)),
                                      modes=(0, 1, 2, 3), n_query=400, dtype=torch.float64)
    amplitudes.append(max(float(s.targets["velocity"].abs().max()),
                          float(s.targets["pressure"].abs().max())))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.4, 3.8))
ax.semilogy(couplings, amplitudes, "o-", color=INK, ms=4, lw=1.4)
ax.axvline(2.405, color=RED, ls=":", lw=1.6)
ax.text(2.36, 60, "$j_{0,1}$: interior no longer\ndetermined by boundary data",
        ha="right", fontsize=9, color=RED)
for lo, hi, label, y in ((0.5, 1.8, "training band", 4.4), (1.9, 2.2, "unseen\ncoupling", 4.0),
                         (2.25, 2.38, "near\neigenvalue", 12.0)):
    ax.axvspan(lo, hi, color=MUTED, alpha=0.12)
    ax.text((lo + hi) / 2, y, label, ha="center", fontsize=8, color=INK2)
ax.set_xlabel(r"vorticity coupling $\tilde c$ [-]")
ax.set_ylabel("max |target| [-] (log)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The third instance of the degree wall holds bitwise: twelve of twelve
linear-arm pressure cells read 1.000. Nonlinear mode breaks it (0.181),
parity channels nearly halve that again (0.103) even though no parity
wall exists for a polar-in, polar-out map, because the problem's natural
latent, $\psi^2$, is a pseudoscalar squared. The linear arm's velocity
is not merely competitive: at 0.026 it beats the nonlinear arms 2.3x
in-distribution and stays at 0.20 on the near-eigenvalue tier where they
reach $10^{9}$–$10^{12}$. Because the velocity map is representable in
every mode, that blowup prices the mode, not the problem. The
declared-degree arm keeps the linear arm's graceful extrapolation while
supplying the pressure (0.106 in-distribution; 0.686 near the
eigenvalue, the amplitude residue discussed above).

### Liouville: the superposition wall, and a contract that is exactly wrong {#sec-liouville}

**A drive-linear model cannot beat its best linear approximation of a
nonlinear solution operator; on this suite that wall sits at 0.769 and
no capacity moves it, while the declared nonlinear mode reaches 0.46.**
Star-deformed disks carry Dirichlet data for
$\Delta u + 2e^{u} = 0$, whose exact solutions are the spherical-metric
potentials $u = \log\big(4|f'|^2/(1+|f|^2)^2\big)$ for holomorphic $f$
(the constant 2 is autograd-verified as a unit test). Solutions are
strictly superharmonic, so interior values exceed the harmonic extension
of the trace everywhere; no map linear in the data can be exact.
Splits: in-distribution, unseen geometry modes, stronger deformation.

The suite also carries the sharpest lesson about zero preservation. Take
$f(w) = w$ on the unit disk: the exact solution
$u = \log\big(4/(1+|w|^2)^2\big)$ has identically zero boundary data and
$u(0) = \log 4 \approx 1.386$ at the center. Every zero-preserving model,
linear or nonlinear, at any capacity, returns exactly zero on this
problem and scores relative error exactly 1. Zero preservation is exact
structure for the linear class and exactly wrong here.

```{python}
#| label: fig-liouville-zerodata
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Zero data, nonzero solution: the exact Liouville solution on the unit
#|   disk with identically zero Dirichlet data (black ring) and log 4 at
#|   the center; right, its radial profile against the output of every
#|   zero-preserving model, which is the flat line at zero. On the general
#|   samples of the suite, whose data are nonzero, the zero-point error is
#|   graded rather than total. Not shown: any trained model.
#| code-fold: true
theta = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 240)
r = np.linspace(0, 1.0, 90)
R, T = np.meshgrid(r, theta)
Xd, Yd = R * np.cos(T), R * np.sin(T)
U = np.log(4.0 / (1.0 + R**2) ** 2)

fig, (ax, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.2, 4.2), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.15, 1]})
cs = ax.contourf(Xd, Yd, U, levels=np.linspace(0, np.log(4), 21), cmap=SEQ_PURPLE)
ax.plot(np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta), color=INK, lw=3.2)
ax.annotate("boundary data $g \\equiv 0$", xy=(np.cos(0.8), np.sin(0.8)), xytext=(1.12, 1.12),
            fontsize=10, color=INK, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=INK2, lw=0.9))
ax.annotate(r"$u(0) = \log 4$", xy=(0, 0), xytext=(-1.55, -1.2), fontsize=10, color=INK,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=INK2, lw=0.9))
fig.colorbar(cs, ax=ax, shrink=0.8, label="exact solution $u$ [-]")
ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_axis_off()

radial = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
ax2.plot(radial, np.log(4.0 / (1.0 + radial**2) ** 2), color=INK, lw=2.4)
ax2.axhline(0.0, color=PURPLE, lw=2.4)
ax2.text(0.03, np.log(4) - 0.06, "exact solution $u(r)$", color=INK, fontsize=10, va="top")
ax2.text(0.03, 0.05, "every zero-preserving model\n(and the harmonic extension of $g$)",
         color=PURPLE, fontsize=10, va="bottom")
ax2.set_xlabel("radius $r$ [-]")
ax2.set_ylabel("$u$ [-]")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The arms below share the fixed-compute protocol of every Liouville
baseline: 1,500 streamed steps, seeds 17/18/19, in-distribution relative
$L^2$ error. The strong-form column is
$\|\Delta \hat u + 2e^{\hat u}\| / \|e^{\hat u}\|$ of the prediction on
32 interior points of two cases, where the exact solution scores 0 and
any harmonic prediction scores exactly 2.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-liouville-arms
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
it8 = bie["iteration_8_liouville_nonlinear_wall"]
rep = it8["replication_p2b"]["summary_1500_steps_3_seeds"]
arms17 = it8["arms_seed17"]
rows = [("MT1, linear mode (wall control)", "mesh_transformer_kernel_linear", "linear_ID"),
        ("MT1, nonlinear mode, two exact members + 8 learned smooth members", "mesh_transformer_kernel_nl", "nl_ID"),
        ("MT1, nonlinear mode, dictionary only (no learned members)", "mesh_transformer_kernel_nl_nomlp", "nl_nomlp_ID")]
lines = ["| arm | parameters | seed 17 | seed 18 | seed 19 | mean | strong-form residual (seed 17) |",
         "|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|"]
for label, key17, keyrep in rows:
    vals = rep[keyrep]
    lines.append(f"| {label} | {arms17[key17]['parameters']:,} | "
                 + " | ".join(f"{v:.3f}" for v in vals)
                 + f" | {sum(vals) / len(vals):.3f} | {arms17[key17]['pde_residual']:.2f} |")
sing = bie["iteration_13_singonly_universality"]["liouville_nl_singonly_1500steps"]["runs"]
lines.append("| MT1, nonlinear mode, double-layer member only | — | "
             + " | ".join(f"{r['in_distribution']:.2f}" for r in sing) + " | unstable | — |")
lines.append(": Liouville in-distribution relative $L^2$ error, 1,500 steps. The "
             "archive records the drive-linear superposition bound at about 0.79; "
             "the linear arm lands on it. The last row's seed 18 detonates to 36.5: "
             "the exact-members-only dictionary that wins every linear suite is "
             "unstable on a nonlinear one. Data: results/learned_bie_2026-07-02.json, "
             "keys `iteration_8_liouville_nonlinear_wall` and "
             "`iteration_13_singonly_universality`. {#tbl-liouville-arms}")
print("\n".join(lines))
```


Three facts carry beyond this suite. The wall is representational and
shared: the linear control is the same architecture minus permission to
read drive invariants, so the 0.769-to-0.464 gap is attributable to drive
nonlinearity alone. The field is fit while the operator is not: the
nonlinear arms' strong-form residual (3.0) is farther from the operator
than the linear control's (2.3) even as their $L^2$ error halves, so the
nonlinear correction bends the field toward the data, not toward
$\Delta u = -2e^{u}$. And the dictionary lesson inverts: exact members
alone suffice on every linear suite, but a nonlinear read-in needs learned
smooth members to stay stable.

The stream factorization (@sec-stream-factorization) prices the
zero-preservation misspecification directly. At matched parameters, MT1's
operator/drive two-stream form and a single-stream control that forfeits
the zero-drive contract tie on nonlinear Liouville (0.533 ± 0.145 vs
0.478 ± 0.097 in-distribution, 3 seeds), while the two-stream arm's
response to zero drive is exactly 0 and the control learns 0.55–0.70,
the physically correct nonzero answer. On the linear Laplace suite the
same factorization wins in-distribution (0.0485 vs 0.0606) with
roundoff-exact contracts. The general statement: **a structural prior
needs a per-problem correctness check, because a contract can be exactly
enforced and exactly wrong.**

## Navier–Stokes star cavity: the solver-labelled viscous suite {#sec-part-ns}

**With solver labels whose noise floor is measured three decades below
model error, the degree wall becomes a function of Reynolds number: the
linear mode's pressure gap to the nonlinear mode is zero in the
near-Stokes band and 0.45–0.54 in the convection-dominated band, and its
velocity gap, once parity channels are matched, follows the same graded
shape at a tenth the height.** This is the suite where exactness ends
and the industrial datasets' conditions begin.

### The problem and its label credential {#sec-ds-navier-stokes}

Star-shaped cavities from the book's geometry family hold viscous fluid
driven by a tangential wall-velocity band: a generalized lid-driven
cavity whose lid is a smooth arc-length window of moving wall (25–50% of
the perimeter, a $C^\infty$ bump times a band-limited modulation, unit
peak speed), randomized in position, width and profile. The flow solves
steady incompressible Navier–Stokes,

$$
(u\cdot\nabla)u = -\nabla p + \tfrac{1}{\mathrm{Re}}\Delta u,
\qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,
\qquad u = g \ \text{on } \partial\Omega,
$$

with unit reference length so $\mathrm{Re} = 1/\nu$ exactly; the model
receives $\tilde\nu = 1/\mathrm{Re}$ as a global operator scalar. A
tangential drive has zero normal flux pointwise, so the incompressibility
compatibility condition holds exactly at the continuous level. Targets
are velocity and pressure at 128 interior queries (wall distance at least
0.12) plus 32 near-wall queries (distance 0.02–0.08). The production
catalog has 1,400 cases: 840 train and 140 in-distribution evaluation
cases at $\mathrm{Re} \in [10, 200]$ (log-uniform), and 140 each for
unseen Reynolds number $(200, 300]$, unseen geometry (deformation
0.45–0.65), and unseen drive profile (modulation modes 3–5 against the
training 0–2).

```{python}
#| label: fig-ns-sample
#| fig-cap: >
#|   One training case as posed: the cavity wall colored by tangential
#|   drive speed (the moving band; the rest is no-slip), the 160 query
#|   points inside with the near-wall band visible, and the case's own
#|   certification. Every case in the catalog carries these numbers. Not
#|   shown: the solution fields, which @fig-ns-gallery carries. Data:
#|   datasets/ns_cavity_star/v1/case_00000.npz.
#| code-fold: true
CATALOG = Path("..") / "datasets" / "ns_cavity_star" / "v1"
case = np.load(CATALOG / "case_00000.npz")
params = json.loads(str(case["__params__"]))
pts = case["boundary_points"]; cells = case["boundary_cells"]
speed = np.linalg.norm(case["boundary_velocity"], axis=1)
queries = case["query_points"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 5.6))
norm = Normalize(0, speed.max())
segs = pts[cells]
ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segs, colors=SEQ_PURPLE(norm(speed)), linewidths=3.6,
                                 capstyle="round", zorder=3))
ax.plot(queries[:, 0], queries[:, 1], ".", color=INK, ms=3.5)
driven = speed > 0.05 * speed.max()
band_mid = segs[driven].mean(axis=(0, 1))
ax.annotate("moving-wall band\n(tangential drive)", xy=tuple(band_mid), xytext=(0.02, 0.97),
            textcoords="axes fraction", fontsize=10, color=INK, va="top",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=INK2, lw=0.9))
ver = params["verification"]
ax.text(0.98, 0.02,
        "this case's certification:\n"
        f"Newton residual {ver['relative_residual']:.1e}\n"
        f"momentum balance {ver['momentum_balance_error']:.1e}\n"
        f"velocity noise floor {ver['label_noise_floor_velocity']:.1e}\n"
        f"pressure noise floor {ver['label_noise_floor_pressure']:.1e}",
        transform=ax.transAxes, ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color=INK2,
        bbox=dict(facecolor="#f4f3ef", edgecolor=GRID))
fig.colorbar(plt.cm.ScalarMappable(cmap=SEQ_PURPLE, norm=norm), ax=ax, shrink=0.7,
             label="wall speed $|g|$ [-]")
ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
for spine in ax.spines.values():
    spine.set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

A solver-labelled suite is only as good as its labels, and model errors
near $10^{-1}$ demand labels at least an order better. The solver is a
Taylor–Hood P2–P1 finite-element discretization with exact-Jacobian
Newton, a Stokes initial guess, backtracking and viscosity continuation,
a zero-mean pressure gauge, and direct linear solves. Its credential has
four legs: manufactured-solution convergence order and accuracy, a
finer-mesh re-solve on a deterministic subset that bounds the *label
noise floor* (the relative change of the labels under mesh refinement by
1.5x), and the discrete balance identities of every case.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ns-verification

    ("manufactured-solution convergence order (unit square)", "velocity ~3, pressure ~2",
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-ns-gallery
#| fig-cap: >
#|   How the Reynolds number grades the family: velocity magnitude of the
#|   finite-element solution for three samples (rows; geometry and drive
#|   pinned within each row, re-solved at four Reynolds numbers) across
#|   Re = 10, 50, 150, 300 (columns), wall ring colored by tangential drive
#|   speed. Color is square-root-scaled in speed on one shared scale so
#|   that the thin wall jet near speed 1 does not hide the cavity-scale
#|   recirculation near speed 0.1. Reading across a row, the wall jet
#|   penetrates further and the recirculation loses its Stokes-flow
#|   symmetry as Re grows. Not shown: the pressure, and any model output.
#|   Data: book/archive/data/ns_gallery_fields_2026-07-07.npz (h = 0.02 solves).
#| code-fold: true
import matplotlib.tri as mtri
from matplotlib.colors import PowerNorm

GALLERY = np.load(Path("data") / "ns_gallery_fields_2026-07-07.npz")
seeds = GALLERY["geometry_seeds"]
res = GALLERY["reynolds_values"]


def smooth_panel(ax, k, show_re=None):
    tri = mtri.Triangulation(GALLERY[f"case{k}_points"][:, 0], GALLERY[f"case{k}_points"][:, 1],
                             triangles=GALLERY[f"case{k}_triangles"])
    speed = np.linalg.norm(GALLERY[f"case{k}_velocity"], axis=1)
    ax.tripcolor(tri, speed, shading="gouraud", cmap=SEQ_PURPLE,
                 norm=PowerNorm(0.5, vmin=0.0, vmax=1.0), rasterized=True)
    loop = GALLERY[f"case{k}_loop"]
    wall = GALLERY[f"case{k}_wall_speed"]
    closed = np.vstack([loop, loop[:1]])
    segs = np.stack([closed[:-1], closed[1:]], axis=1)
    ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segs, colors="#9a988f", linewidths=0.9, capstyle="round", zorder=3))
    driven = wall > 0.02
    if driven.any():
        ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segs[driven],
                                         colors=SEQ_PURPLE(PowerNorm(0.5, vmin=0, vmax=1)(wall[driven])),
                                         linewidths=2.6, capstyle="round", zorder=4))
    lo_b, hi_b = loop.min(axis=0), loop.max(axis=0)
    mid, half = (lo_b + hi_b) / 2, (hi_b - lo_b).max() / 2 * 1.06
    ax.set_xlim(mid[0] - half, mid[0] + half); ax.set_ylim(mid[1] - half, mid[1] + half)
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
    for spine in ax.spines.values():
        spine.set_visible(False)
    if show_re is not None:
        ax.set_title(rf"$\mathrm{{Re}} = {show_re:.0f}$", fontsize=9, color=INK)


fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(seeds), len(res), figsize=(9.4, 7.4))
for row_i in range(len(seeds)):
    for col in range(len(res)):
        smooth_panel(axes[row_i, col], row_i * len(res) + col, show_re=res[col] if row_i == 0 else None)
    axes[row_i, 0].set_ylabel(f"sample {row_i + 1}", fontsize=9, color=INK2)
    axes[row_i, 0].yaxis.set_visible(True)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### Arms, and the Reynolds-graded wall {#sec-ns-cavity}

For Navier–Stokes the solution map is analytic in the drive with every
polynomial order present: the Stokes component is drive-linear and each
convection correction raises the degree. The linear mode's wall is
therefore a function of Reynolds number rather than an all-or-nothing
barrier, and the declared-degree mode is an approximation hypothesis.
Five arms train on the 840-case split for 15 epochs at 3 seeds, and each
arm restores its best-validation checkpoint before the test-split
evaluation (the one suite in this book where checkpoint selection uses
validation error; the industrial recipe evaluates final-epoch checkpoints,
@sec-protocol): MT1 in
linear mode, nonlinear mode with parity channels, declared degree 2 with
parity channels, the boundary-mean predictor, and Transolver
(@sec-transolver) at matched parameter count (103,375 against
106,408–233,108 for the MT1 arms) on the same token contract
(coordinates, normals, panel measures, the rank-1 drive, and $\tilde\nu$
as a constant channel). Transolver receives the same 15-epoch budget on
the same 840 cases, a budget that may undertrain it, so its gap to the
MT1 arms is an upper bound on the converged gap. All MT1 arms use the
one-head configuration and the two exact members. Cells are the combined
velocity-and-pressure relative $L^2$ error, mean ± sd over seeds.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ns-arms
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
arms = suite["arms"]
order = ["mt_singpair_q2_pseudo", "mt_singpair_nl_pseudo", "mt_singpair_linear",
         "transolver_intree_matched", "boundary_mean"]
labels = {"mt_singpair_q2_pseudo": "MT1, declared degree 2 + parity channels",
          "mt_singpair_nl_pseudo": "**MT1, nonlinear mode + parity channels**",
          "mt_singpair_linear": "MT1, linear mode (wall control)",
          "transolver_intree_matched": "Transolver, matched parameters",
          "boundary_mean": "boundary-mean predictor (floor)"}

split_names = ["in-distribution", "unseen Re", "unseen geometry", "unseen drive"]
headers = ["arm", "parameters"] + split_names
print("| " + " | ".join(headers) + " |")
print("|---|--:|" + "--:|" * len(splits))
for arm in order:
    row_cells = [labels[arm], f"{arms[arm]['parameters']:,}"]
    for split in splits:
        cell = arms[arm]["splits"][split]["combined"]
        row_cells.append(f"{cell['mean']:.3f} ± {cell['sd']:.3f}")
    print("| " + " | ".join(row_cells) + " |")
print()
n_train = suite["dataset"]["split_sizes"]["train"]
print(": Navier–Stokes cavity, combined relative $L^2$ error, mean ± sd over 3 "
      f"seeds, 15 epochs on the {n_train}-case train split, 140 cases per "
      "evaluation split. Per-field and near-wall values are in the artifact; "
      "@fig-ns-wall shows the per-field Reynolds dependence. The Transolver row "
      "is trained for the same 15 epochs on the same 840 cases as the MT1 arms, "
      "a budget that may undertrain it, so its gap to the MT1 arms is an upper "
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-ns-wall
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The Reynolds-graded wall on the production catalog: per-case relative
#|   L2 error pooled over the in-distribution and unseen-Re splits (3
#|   seeds), binned by case Reynolds number in five log bins, velocity
#|   left and pressure right. The pressure gap between the linear mode and
#|   the nonlinear arms grows 4.2x from the lowest to the highest bin; the
#|   velocity gap is flat near 0.19 across Re 10–300, which @sec-ns-lowre
#|   resolves. How to read this: the gap between arms, not the absolute
#|   level, is the wall; all arms share dataset, protocol and seeds. Data:
#|   results/ns_cavity_star_2026-07-05.json.
#| code-fold: true
wall = suite["re_wall"]["per_arm"]
style = {
    "mt_singpair_linear": (PURPLE_LIGHT, "o--", "MT1, linear mode"),
    "mt_singpair_nl_pseudo": (PURPLE, "^-", "MT1, nonlinear + parity"),
    "mt_singpair_q2_pseudo": (PURPLE_DARK, "s-", "MT1, declared degree 2 + parity"),
    "transolver_intree_matched": (TRANSOLVER, "d-", "Transolver"),
}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.4, 3.8), sharex=True)
for ax, field in zip(axes, ("velocity", "pressure")):
    ends = []
    for arm, (color, marker, label) in style.items():
        entry = wall[arm]
        ax.loglog(entry["bin_centers"], entry[field], marker, ms=4, lw=1.3, color=color)
        ends.append((entry["bin_centers"][-1], entry[field][-1], label, color))
    floor = wall["boundary_mean"]
    ax.loglog(floor["bin_centers"], floor[field], ":", lw=1.2, color=INK)
    ends.append((floor["bin_centers"][-1], floor[field][-1], "boundary-mean floor", INK))
    x_end = floor["bin_centers"][-1]
    ax.set_ylim(top=ax.get_ylim()[1] * 1.6)  # headroom for the label stack
    direct_labels(ax, ends, x_text=x_end * 1.18, min_gap=0.075)
    ax.set_xlim(right=x_end * 6.0)
    ax.set_xlabel("case Reynolds number [-]")
    ax.set_ylabel(f"{field} relative $L^2$ [-]")
    ax.set_title(field, fontsize=9)
    ax.grid(which="both")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Three preregistered rules decide the figure. The pressure gap between
the linear mode and the nonlinear arms grows from 0.11 in the lowest bin
to 0.47 in the highest (ratio 4.2, bar 3): the graded wall. The
declared-degree arm is within twice the seed standard deviation of the
nonlinear arm in-distribution (0.278 ± 0.060 vs 0.231 ± 0.005), but
behind it on every split: a degree-2 truncation is short where all
orders are present. The boundary-mean predictor's pressure error is
exactly 1.000, because the pressure has zero mean by gauge. The velocity
gap, however, is flat at about 0.19 from Re 10 to Re 300 rather than
vanishing toward the Stokes limit. Re 10 at unit drive speed is not
Stokes, so the production catalog cannot decide whether the flat gap is
physics or a deficit of the linear read-in.

### The near-Stokes band, and what the velocity gap was {#sec-ns-lowre}

**In the near-Stokes band the linear mode matches the nonlinear mode on
velocity once parity channels are matched; the flat velocity gap on the
production catalog was a missing parity sector, not the read-in class.**
A supplementary catalog slice of 180 cases (108 train, 18 per evaluation
split) moves only the Reynolds axis: train and in-distribution at
$\mathrm{Re}$ log-uniform in $[0.5, 5]$, unseen Reynolds at $(5, 10]$,
with the production geometry, drive family, mesh resolution and
certification. Three arms train on it and on the production catalog at
the identical protocol: the linear mode, the nonlinear mode with parity
channels, and the *fair control*, the linear mode plus the same parity
sector as the nonlinear arm. Parameters are 106,408, 233,108 and
131,248; the parity sector adds 24,840 parameters, and the remaining
difference to the nonlinear arm is the nonlinear read-in stack, which is
the treatment variable. The per-case gap of each arm to the nonlinear
reference joins across the two catalogs into one curve from Re 0.5 to
300; each side is internally controlled, so the gap crosses the catalog
seam even though absolute errors do not.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ns-lowre-gap
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The gap to the nonlinear reference (arm minus nonlinear-with-parity,
#|   per-case mean per log-Re bin, in-distribution and unseen-Re pooled
#|   over 3 seeds) across Re 0.5–300, velocity left and pressure right.
#|   Filled circles: the low-Re slice (108-case train split); open squares:
#|   the production catalog (840-case train split); dashed vertical line:
#|   the catalog seam. The plain linear mode's velocity gap is flat at
#|   0.13–0.23 everywhere, including the drive-linear band; the fair
#|   control (same linear read-in plus parity channels) collapses it to zero
#|   or below across the near-Stokes band and leaves a graded remainder
#|   rising to 0.10–0.12 by Re 100–213. Both arms' pressure gaps are zero at
#|   low Re and grow to about 0.5: no parity sector rescues a drive-linear
#|   read-in from a drive-nonlinear target. Not shown: absolute errors,
#|   which @tbl-ns-arms and @tbl-ns-lowre carry. Data:
#|   results/ns_linear_pseudo_confound_2026-07-05.json.
#| code-fold: true
confound = json.load(open(RESULTS / "ns_linear_pseudo_confound_2026-07-05.json"))
joined = confound["re_gap_curves"]["joined"]
seam = 10.0
gap_arms = (("mt_singpair_linear", PURPLE_LIGHT, "MT1, linear mode (106k)"),
            ("mt_singpair_linear_pseudo", PURPLE_DARK, "MT1, linear mode + parity channels (131k)"))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.4, 3.8), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, field in zip(axes, ("velocity", "pressure")):
    low_edge = min(joined[gap_arms[0][0]]["bin_centers"]) / 1.4
    ax.axvspan(low_edge, 1.0, color="#eceaf4", zorder=0)
    ax.axhline(0.0, color=GRID, lw=1.0, zorder=1)
    ax.axvline(seam, color=BASELINE, lw=1.0, ls="--", zorder=1)
    ends = []
    for arm, color, label in gap_arms:
        entry = joined[arm]
        centers = np.array(entry["bin_centers"])
        values = np.array(entry[f"{field}_gap"])
        catalog = np.array(entry["catalog"])
        ax.plot(centers, values, "-", lw=1.3, color=color, zorder=2)
        for cat, marker, face in (("v1-lowre", "o", color), ("v1", "s", "white")):
            mask = catalog == cat
            ax.plot(centers[mask], values[mask], marker, ms=5, lw=0, color=color,
                    markerfacecolor=face, markeredgecolor=color, zorder=3)
        ends.append((centers[-1], values[-1], label, color))
    direct_labels(ax, ends, x_text=centers[-1] * 1.25, min_gap=0.05, log_y=False)
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set_xlim(right=centers[-1] * 40.0)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.17, 0.6)
    ax.set_xlabel("case Reynolds number [-]")
    ax.set_title(f"{field} gap to the nonlinear reference", fontsize=9)
    ax.grid(which="both", axis="x")
axes[0].set_ylabel("arm $-$ nonlinear reference, relative $L^2$ [-]")
axes[0].text(0.6, -0.163, "near-Stokes\n(drive-linear)", fontsize=7.5, color=INK2, ha="left", va="bottom")
axes[0].text(90.0, -0.163, "convection-dominated", fontsize=7.5, color=INK2, ha="center", va="bottom")
axes[0].annotate("catalog seam", (seam, 0.34), xytext=(3, 0), textcoords="offset points",
                 fontsize=7, color=INK2, rotation=90, va="bottom")
axes[0].text(0.5, 0.56, "filled circles: low-Re slice; open squares: production catalog",
             fontsize=7.5, color=INK2, va="top")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The preregistered rule for the fair control was a bottom-bin velocity
gap at or below 0.05 (parity, not read-in class) against at or above 0.1
(read-in class). Measured: $-0.024$, with the plain linear mode's 0.184
reproduced bin for bin in the same rerun. With the confound removed the
velocity gap has the graded shape the physics predicts, near zero across
Re 0.5–7 and 0.10–0.12 at Re 100–213. The pressure sharpens the same
statement from the other side: the parity sector does nothing for the
pressure gap (0.016 at the bottom bin, 0.45–0.54 at the top, bin for bin
the plain linear mode's curve), and on the production catalog the
nonlinear arm still wins pressure decisively (0.356 vs 0.684
in-distribution). The graded Reynolds-tracking wall is real for both
fields; the velocity's is an order of magnitude smaller than the parity
artefact that sat on top of it. One caveat stands: the fair control
matches the nonlinear arm's sector structure, not its width (131k vs
233k), so capacity and parity are separated from the read-in class but
not from each other.

The low-Re slice also carries the suite's first strong-form fidelity
columns: the momentum residual
$\|\tilde\nu\Delta\hat u - (\hat u\cdot\nabla)\hat u - \nabla\hat p\| /
\|(\hat u\cdot\nabla)\hat u\|$ and the divergence norm of the model's own
prediction, by float64 autograd on 32 interior queries of two cases per
split, with $\tilde\nu$ taken from the case. The instrument is certified
in-tree (the exact Kovasznay solution scores near zero only with the
case's $\tilde\nu$; a rigid rotation with its pressure dropped scores
exactly 1). Near Stokes the true advection is small while $\tilde\nu$ is
order one, so the advection-normalized residual amplifies
second-derivative error; the $O(10)$ values say the predictions'
derivatives do not satisfy the operator, as on every suite.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ns-lowre
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
lowre = confound["arms_lowre"]
order = ["mt_singpair_nl_pseudo", "mt_singpair_linear_pseudo", "mt_singpair_linear"]
labels = {"mt_singpair_nl_pseudo": "MT1, nonlinear mode + parity channels",
          "mt_singpair_linear_pseudo": "MT1, linear mode + parity channels (fair control)",
          "mt_singpair_linear": "MT1, linear mode"}
headers = ["arm", "parameters"] + split_names + ["momentum residual (ID)", "divergence (ID)"]
print("| " + " | ".join(headers) + " |")
print("|---|--:|" + "--:|" * (len(splits) + 2))
for arm in order:
    row_cells = [labels[arm], f"{lowre[arm]['parameters']:,}"]
    for split in splits:
        cell = lowre[arm]["splits"][split]["combined"]
        row_cells.append(f"{cell['mean']:.3f} ± {cell['sd']:.3f}")
    for key in ("momentum_residual", "divergence_residual"):
        cell = lowre[arm]["fidelity"][key]["eval_id"]
        row_cells.append(f"{cell['mean']:.1f} ± {cell['sd']:.1f}")
    print("| " + " | ".join(row_cells) + " |")
print()
n_train = confound["dataset"]["lowre_split_sizes"]["train"]
print(": The near-Stokes slice (Re 0.5–5 train, 5–10 unseen Re): combined "
      f"relative $L^2$ error, mean ± sd over 3 seeds, {n_train}-case train split, "
      "18 cases per evaluation split, with the strong-form fidelity columns. The "
      "three arms tie on combined error in-distribution; the fidelity columns "
      "order them as the velocity gap does, with the plain linear mode 2–3x above "
      "the other two. Data: results/ns_linear_pseudo_confound_2026-07-05.json. "
      "{#tbl-ns-lowre}")
```

### The wide-Reynolds sweep {#sec-ns-reynolds-sweep}

**Accuracy versus Reynolds number is U-shaped across three decades, the
label-noise floor sits three orders of magnitude below model error
everywhere, and the sweep ends where steady solutions stop being
computable.** Three additional log-banded catalogs, generated under the
production verification protocol, place the nonlinear-with-parity arm at
$\mathrm{Re} \in [1, 10]$, $[10, 100]$ and $[100, 1000]$, each trained
at 3 seeds under the frozen protocol, alongside the production band
$[10, 200]$. The table gives the in-distribution combined error (3-seed
median and range), the error on each band's unseen-Reynolds slice
directly above it, and the measured label-noise floor. Unlike every
other table in this chapter, its values have no artifact under
`results/`: they are transcribed from the training-run logs, and the
table and figure below carry that label.

| training band, Re | in-distribution (3-seed) | unseen Re | label-noise floor |
|---|---|---|---|
| [1, 10] | 0.312 (0.275–0.349) | 0.344 | 0.00020 |
| [10, 100] | 0.257 (0.239–0.276) | 0.375 | 0.00021 |
| [10, 200] (production) | 0.230 (0.219–0.239) | 0.358 | 0.00024 |
| [100, 1000] | 0.348 (0.320–0.401) | 0.369 | 0.00038 |

: The Reynolds bands (catalogs `v2-re1`, `v2-re10`, `v1`, `v2-re100`
under `datasets/ns_cavity_star/`), nonlinear-with-parity MT1 arm, 15
epochs, 3 seeds. The unseen-Re penalties are not comparable across
bands, because each band's unseen slice sits at a different relative
distance from its training range. Not reproducible from `results/`;
transcribed from run logs (@sec-nb-e1-curve). {#tbl-ns-reynolds-bands}

```{python}
#| label: fig-ns-reynolds-sweep
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Combined relative L2 error versus Reynolds number for the
#|   nonlinear-with-parity MT1 arm, one independently trained 3-seed arm
#|   per band. Horizontal bars show each band's Reynolds extent (two bands
#|   overlap), vertical bars the seed range, open squares the unseen-Re
#|   slice. The curve is U-shaped: the middle decades are easiest and both
#|   the near-Stokes and advective ends are harder. Lower panel: the
#|   measured label-noise floor, which rises 2x across the sweep and sits
#|   three orders of magnitude below the model error, so it never limits
#|   the result. The shaded region is the measured steady-solver ceiling.
#|   How to read this: the arm and protocol were fixed on the production
#|   band in the middle of the sweep, so the U cannot be separated from
#|   fixed-protocol regime sensitivity without per-band retuning, which
#|   was not done. Not reproducible from results/; values and the solver
#|   ceiling transcribed from run logs, as in @tbl-ns-reynolds-bands.
#| code-fold: true
bands = [
    ("[1, 10]", (1, 10), 0.312, 0.275, 0.349, 0.344, 0.00020),
    ("[10, 100]", (10, 100), 0.257, 0.239, 0.276, 0.375, 0.00021),
    ("[10, 200]", (10, 200), 0.230, 0.219, 0.239, 0.358, 0.00024),
    ("[100, 1000]", (100, 1000), 0.348, 0.320, 0.401, 0.369, 0.00038),
]
centers = [np.sqrt(lo * hi) for _, (lo, hi), *_ in bands]
median = np.array([b[2] for b in bands])
lo_err = median - np.array([b[3] for b in bands])
hi_err = np.array([b[4] for b in bands]) - median
unseen = [b[5] for b in bands]
floor_vals = [b[6] for b in bands]

fig, (ax, ax_floor) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.9, 4.6), sharex=True,
                                   gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [3.1, 1.0], "hspace": 0.12})
for axis in (ax, ax_floor):
    axis.axvspan(4200, 20000, color=RED, alpha=0.07, lw=0)
ax.text(4550, 0.412, "steady-solver\nceiling (measured)", fontsize=7.5, color="#a83a39", va="top")
for (label, (lo, hi), med, *_), center in zip(bands, centers):
    ax.plot([lo, hi], [med, med], color=PURPLE, lw=1.0, alpha=0.45, solid_capstyle="butt", zorder=2)
ax.plot(centers, median, "-", color=PURPLE, lw=1.8, alpha=0.6, zorder=3)
ax.errorbar(centers, median, yerr=[lo_err, hi_err], fmt="o", ms=8, color=PURPLE, ecolor=PURPLE,
            elinewidth=1.4, capsize=4, mec="white", mew=1.2, zorder=4)
ax.plot(centers, unseen, "s", ms=6.5, mfc="none", mec=INK2, mew=1.6, zorder=4)
label_offsets = {"[1, 10]": (40, 8), "[10, 200]": (16, -15), "[10, 100]": (-44, 14),
                 "[100, 1000]": (58, -14)}
for (label, *_), center, med in zip(bands, centers, median):
    dx, dy = label_offsets[label]
    ax.annotate(f"Re {label}", (center, med), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(dx, dy),
                ha="center", fontsize=8, color=INK2)
ax.annotate("unseen-Re slice\n(open squares)", (centers[0], unseen[0]), textcoords="offset points",
            xytext=(-6, 26), ha="center", fontsize=8, color=INK2,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=INK2, lw=0.7))
ax.annotate("in-band evaluation:\n3-seed median and range", (centers[0], median[0] - lo_err[0]),
            xytext=(1.05, 0.204), textcoords="data", ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=8,
            color=PURPLE, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=PURPLE, lw=0.7, shrinkB=2))
ax.set_ylim(0.20, 0.45)
ax.set_ylabel("combined relative $L^2$ [-]")
ax_floor.plot(centers, floor_vals, "-o", color=MUTED, lw=1.5, ms=5, zorder=3)
ax_floor.set_ylim(1.2e-4, 9e-4)
ax_floor.set_yscale("log")
ax_floor.set_yticks([2e-4, 4e-4, 8e-4], ["2e-4", "4e-4", "8e-4"])
ax_floor.minorticks_off()
ax_floor.set_ylabel("noise floor [-]")
ax_floor.set_xscale("log")
ax_floor.set_xlim(0.8, 12000)
ax_floor.set_xlabel("Reynolds number [-]")
plt.show()
```

The confound is part of the current understanding, not a footnote: the
arm and protocol were tuned on the production band $[10, 200]$, the
middle of the sweep, so the U may measure fixed-protocol regime
sensitivity rather than intrinsic difficulty, and the two are not
separable without per-band retuning, which the program's rule against
protocol tuning reserves for an experiment about the protocol itself.
The floor measurement settles a different question: labels are not what
limits this suite anywhere in the sweep.

The sweep stops for a physical reason. Generating a $[1000, 10000]$ band
reached 450 cases before an unseen-split case drawing
$\mathrm{Re} \in [4166, 4667]$ stalled the Newton solve on all eight
retry attempts, while every case at $\mathrm{Re} \le 4000$ solved
cleanly; bracket probes place the onset of stalls near
$\mathrm{Re} \approx 4200$, thickening toward 5000. These counts come
from the generator's logs, not from a `results/` artifact.^[Notebook
record: @sec-nb-re-ceiling-final.] Steady cavity solutions stop being
practically computable there, and that is a measured limit of the
benchmark rather than of any model.

## What carries across the suites

Four things hold on every suite in this chapter, and they are what the
industrial chapters inherit.

**The walls are decided at the read-in, not in the encoder.** Every wall
here is crossed by changing what the decoder is permitted to read
(drive invariants, a bilinear composition, a parity sector) at a
parameter change of at most a few percent, and none is crossed by width
or depth. Where the target is representable and the inputs are the same,
the encoder does its job well: the trace-driven MT1 (about 105k
parameters) reaches 0.013 on the exterior problem against 0.178 for the
19,008-parameter trace-informed pair-kernel control given the same
boundary trace, and the linear mode is the best velocity model on
rotational Euler. The
one-head configuration and the two exact kernel members (@sec-mt1) are
used unchanged on all five suites; the one dictionary lesson that
changes with nonlinearity is that a nonlinear read-in needs learned
smooth members to stay stable, where exact members alone suffice on
every linear suite.

**Declarations compose.** Parity typing, drive nonlinearity or declared
degree, and the linear-mode-grade equivariance are orthogonal
declarations that multiply on one arm; the axes that need two of them
(circulation-OOD on Euler–Bernoulli, pressure on rotational Euler) show
it, and no single declaration substitutes for another.

**Declared degree is safe where the degree is known and short where it
is not.** It is more accurate and far more stable than the nonlinear
mode on the exact Euler suites, and behind it on Navier–Stokes. The
nonlinear mode's implicit degree near 21 is a standing hazard wherever
the drive can leave its training range.

**The parameter-free floor is the reference.** Where the archive records
it (rotational Euler, Navier–Stokes), the boundary-mean predictor
appears in the table, and the pressure floor of exactly 1.000 under a
zero-mean gauge is the calibration against which the linear mode's
pressure wall is read. The earlier exact-label archives (Liouville,
potential flow, Euler–Bernoulli) do not record a boundary-mean row;
their no-response rows at 1.0 serve the same role.

## Where these suites stop

Everything here is two-dimensional, steady and laminar, with sixteen to
a few hundred evaluation cases per split and labels that are exact or
certified to $10^{-3}$. The Navier–Stokes suite reaches Reynolds 1,000
in training and is bounded by a steady solver near 4,200. None of the
suites has separated flow, a wake, or a three-dimensional surface, and
none has the sampling density, label noise or case-count regime of an
industrial surface-pressure dataset. The industrial datasets add exactly
those conditions: solver-labelled three-dimensional aerodynamics on
hundreds to thousands of cases, where MT1's potential-flow prior fails
on separated flow and the trace formulation carries the gain
(@sec-industrial-mt1), and the data-efficiency comparison against
GeoTransolver and Transolver in which the equivariant soft-slice
MeshTransformer2 replaces the exact kernels (@sec-data-efficiency). The
limits chapter (@sec-limits) collects what this chapter's suites cannot
speak to.
